prime.problem: The scores card leaves each token with a row of weights saying how much to listen to each earlier token, but no content to listen to. Without a way to turn those weights into a new vector, no information moves between tokens.
prime.fits: Builds on attention scores (QKᵀ/√d and the causal mask) and softmax, which turns each score row into shares. This card uses those shares to blend value vectors, then hands the result to the residual on the next card.
expect: context vectors C = A·V (a weighted average)
prime.goal: Compute a row of C and an entry of o by hand from the tiny model's arrays, explain why the weights must sum to 1 and why values are separate from keys, and give the head shapes for GPT-2 and Qwen2.5-0.5B.

attend: Why does row 0 of C come out identical to row 0 of V, and what would have to change for it not to?
What exactly goes wrong in size if the attention weights are raw exp(S) instead of shares that sum to 1, and how does it depend on prompt length?
Key and value come from the same row of a: what does having two separate weight matrices let the model learn that one matrix couldn't?
What can two heads do for one token that a single softmax row can't, and why does that need Wo afterwards?
In Qwen, 14 query heads share 2 value heads: which matrices shrink, and which stay full size?

must: softmax divides by the row sum → each row of A is positive and sums to 1 → C_i = Σ A_ij V_j is a weighted average → every entry stays between the smallest and largest value in its column, whatever the prompt length (raw exp weights made C row 2 9.0926× too big; at 1,024 random tokens 781.92 vs at most 8.000)
causal mask zeroes the future → token 0 has A row 0 = [1, 0, 0] → C row 0 = V row 0 exactly; token 2 has [0.1737, 0.8132, 0.0131] → C2 = [0.9664, 0.5219, 0.7895, −0.4436], mostly cat's value

K = a·Wk and V = a·Wv come from the same input through different weights → the model learns separately what a token is matched on and what it passes along → one matrix would force the matching features and the content to be the same numbers

one softmax row = one blend → a token can't pull different things from different tokens at once → split d into H heads of d/H, each with its own A → concatenate back to d columns → Wo mixes the heads so each one can reach every output column
elevated: o has the same shape as the input x0 (T × d) → it can be added straight back as x1 = x0 + o → the residual on the next card depends on Wo restoring that shape

Grouped-query attention shares one value (and key) head across several query heads → Qwen's V is 7 × 128 instead of 7 × 896 → fewer numbers to store per token in the KV cache, while there are still 14 different A matrices
reference: Qwen2.5-0.5B: 14 query heads, 2 KV heads, head dim 64; Wv 896 × 128, Wo 896 × 896
bo starts at all zeros; Raschka builds context vectors in §3.4.1 and multi-head attention in §3.6

compress.prompt: From memory, explain in 3–5 sentences how attention turns weights into an output vector, and why the weights sum to 1. Or redraw A · V = C for row 2 with the three weighted value rows.
checklist: values are a·Wv, separate from the keys used for matching
each row of C is a weighted average of value rows, weights from that row of A
weights sum to 1, so the output stays on the values' scale at any prompt length
the mask makes row 0 copy V row 0
heads split the columns so one token can make several blends; concatenate, then Wo mixes

retrieve.q: Explain what a context vector is, in terms of the value rows and one row of attention weights.
answer: one row of C per token
it is the sum of the value rows, each scaled by that token's weight on it
because the weights are shares summing to 1, it is a weighted average

retrieve.q: Walk through how the tiny model gets from a and A to o for token 2, naming each matrix and its shape.
answer: o is 3 × 4, the same shape as x0, ready to be added back

retrieve.q: You could give a model 1 head of 768 columns or 12 heads of 64. What does splitting buy, and what does each head give up?
answer: 12 heads give each token 12 separate blends, so it can attend to different tokens for different purposes
each head's scores come from only 64 columns, so each match is made on less information
Wo is needed afterwards to mix the heads back together; the total width stays 768

compare.q: The scores card and this card both multiply by a matrix built from the tokens. What does Q·Kᵀ produce versus A·V, and which one decides who and which decides what?
answer: Q·Kᵀ gives T × T scores: who matches whom
A·V gives T × d: the content that flows
the mask and √d act on the scores; the values are untouched until the blend
a bug in the scores shows up as wrong weights; a bug in V shows up as wrong content with the right weights

compare.q: Karpathy starts with a plain running mean of the past tokens. How does that differ from A·V here, and what does the learned version fix?
answer: the plain mean gives every earlier token equal weight
here the weights come from softmax of learned scores, so they depend on the tokens
both are averages whose weights sum to 1
the learned version lets a token listen mostly to the one that matters (0.8132 on cat)

predict.q: Suppose all of sat's scores were equal instead of [0.4570, 2.0006, −2.1253]. What would A row 2 be, and what would C row 2, column 0 come out as?
predict.answer: Equal scores give equal shares, [1/3, 1/3, 1/3]. Column 0 would be the plain mean of V's column 0: (−0.1255 + 1.2391 − 1.4760)/3 = −0.1208, instead of 0.9664 when sat leans on cat.

apply.task: Compute o row 1, column 0 by hand. Use C row 1 = [0.5596, −0.0499, 0.1404, 0.4675] and column 0 of Wo = [−0.6, 0.8, −0.2, −0.1], with the bias at 0. Then check it against tiny.out.
apply.done: You get −0.4505, matching o[1,0] in tiny.out.
